theme: The call of Abram; the covenant promise; election and blessing
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 12:1-13:18 slowly. This is one of the most important moments in the Bible, the call of Abram, which sets in motion the entire story of redemption. Notice what God promises, what Abram does, and how Abram’s faith is mingled with very real failure.
settingTheScene: Unit 2 ended at the scattering of Babel and narrowed to one man, Abram. Today the story shifts decisively. From here forward, the Bible focuses on one family through whom God will bring blessing to all the families of the earth. This is the great narrowing that becomes the great expanding. Abram is called out of Ur, away from his land and kindred, to a place he does not know. The promise he receives is unconditional: God will make him a great nation, bless him, and bless all nations through him. Everything in the rest of the Bible, Israel, Christ, the church, flows from this call.
observation: God’s call comes with three commands (“go”) and seven promises, land, nation, blessing, great name, blessing to others, cursing of enemies, blessing of all families.
Abram is 75 years old and childless when he is called. The promise of a great nation requires faith from the start.
Verse 4: “So Abram went, as the LORD had told him.” Obedience is immediate, without discussion.
Abram builds altars at Shechem and Bethel, claiming the land for the LORD by worship before he possesses it.
Famine drives Abram to Egypt, where he lies about Sarai being his sister. The chosen patriarch fails morally almost immediately.
Pharaoh, not Abram, ends up rebuking him. God protects the promise even when Abram does not.
Genesis 13: Lot and Abram separate. Abram gives Lot first choice of land, generosity flowing from trust in God’s promise.
After Lot leaves, God reiterates and expands the promise: “all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.”
interpretation:
Genesis 12 is where the story of redemption truly begins. The first eleven chapters of Genesis are sometimes called the prologue, creation, fall, flood, and Babel. From Genesis 12 onward, the Bible follows one family through whom God will reverse the curse of Babel and bring blessing to all the scattered nations.

Notice the structure of the call. God says three things to Abram: go from your country, go from your kindred, go from your father’s house. Each command requires more sacrifice than the last. Country is general; kindred is closer; father’s house is closest. God strips away every layer of identity Abram has built, geography, ethnicity, family, and asks him to find his identity in God alone. This is what every call of God involves at some level. Discipleship means letting God redefine who you are.

In exchange, God makes seven promises. He will make Abram a great nation, bless him, make his name great, make him a blessing, bless those who bless him, curse those who dishonor him, and bless all the families of the earth in him. Seven is the number of completeness. This is not a partial promise; it is a full, comprehensive commitment. And it is given to a 75-year-old man with a barren wife. From a human standpoint, every promise is impossible.

But Abram goes. Verse 4 is breathtaking in its brevity: “So Abram went, as the LORD had told him.” No negotiation. No clarifying questions. He goes. This is what the New Testament will later call the obedience that comes from faith. Abram does not have full understanding. He has a promise from God, and that is enough.

Yet the chapter is honest about Abram’s failure. As soon as famine strikes, he goes to Egypt, and there he lies about Sarai. He calls her his sister so that the Egyptians will not kill him to take her. The chosen patriarch protects himself by endangering his wife. God has just promised to bless him and curse those who curse him, and Abram does not trust the promise enough to tell the truth. The result is that Pharaoh rebukes Abram. The pagan king has more integrity in this moment than the called patriarch. This is one of the Bible’s repeated patterns: God’s chosen people are real people with real failures, and the promise of God succeeds despite them, not because of them.

Then in chapter 13, after returning to Canaan, conflict arises between Abram’s herdsmen and Lot’s. Abram offers Lot first choice of land. Lot chooses the well-watered Jordan plain near Sodom. Abram is left with the hill country. But notice, after Lot leaves, God speaks again to Abram and expands the promise. “Lift up your eyes and look… for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.” Abram lets go of his rights and God gives him more than he could have grasped for himself. This will be a pattern throughout the patriarchal narratives. Those who trust God do not need to defend their own interests; God defends them.
connection: The scattering of Babel ended Unit 2 with humanity in pieces, alienated from God and from one another. Today’s reading begins the answer. God will reunite the nations not by undoing the scattering but by working through one chosen family. The blessing promised to Abram in verse 3, “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed”, is the New Testament’s gospel in seed form (Galatians 3:8). Every promise made to Abram is eventually fulfilled in Christ, who is the offspring through whom all nations are blessed.
application: The call of Abram is the pattern for every Christian life. God calls. We go. We trust in promises we cannot fully see. We fail along the way, and God’s promise stands anyway. Today, ask yourself: what is God asking you to leave behind? What identity, what comfort, what security has he asked you to release in order to find your life in him alone? And what promise has he given you that you are tempted not to trust? Faith is not the absence of fear or even of failure. It is going when God says go, building altars of worship along the way, and trusting that the same God who called you will keep his word.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what “going” might look like for you, and what makes it hard to trust him with it.
Confess any time you have schemed to protect yourself instead of trusting his promise.
Ask him to make you a person who builds altars of worship wherever he leads.
